turns.text: Can you describe your first night after arriving in Beidahuang? What did you see, hear, and feel as you tried to fall asleep in this new place?

The first night, I remember the cold most of all. The room was a long, low building, mud walls patched with newspaper, and the wind found every crack. I lay on a hard wooden platform, packed in with other girls, our breath making small clouds above us. The blankets smelled of old straw and sweat. I could hear people shifting, coughing, someone quietly crying, but everyone tried to keep quiet so the team leaders wouldn’t notice. The air tasted of damp earth and coal smoke. My legs ached from the train ride and the walk to the settlement, and my mind kept circling back to home—my sisters, the city lights, the sound of trams at night. Here, there was only darkness and the endless rustle of the wind outside. I felt small, as if the land itself was pressing down, and I realized I had no idea when I would see Shanghai again. I didn’t sleep much. I kept thinking about how far I was from everything I knew, and how I had to find a way to survive in this place that didn’t care about my past at all.

The way you describe the cold and the unfamiliar sounds makes it feel so immediate, like the city and everything you knew was suddenly erased. You mentioned the smell of coal smoke and old straw—did certain smells or sounds from Beidahuang ever become comforting to you, or did they always remind you of how far you were from home?

At first, every smell and sound felt foreign, almost hostile. But over time, some of them became a kind of background music to my life. The coal smoke, for example, started to mean warmth in winter—even though it was harsh and made my throat scratchy, it meant someone had managed to get the stove going, and we’d gather around it, talking or just thawing our hands. The sound of the wind in the reeds, which used to keep me awake, eventually became something I listened for at night. It was constant, almost like the city’s traffic used to be. The smell of steamed cornmeal, too, became strangely reassuring, even though I hated eating it at first. I think I started to accept that these things were part of my world now, and maybe I needed them to feel anchored. But the smell of wet earth after rain always made me homesick, because it was so different from the scent of the city after a storm. That feeling never changed.

Reflecting on how some things shifted from alien to familiar, and others always tugged at your longing for home, makes me think about how people adapt in ways they might not expect. You mentioned gathering around the stove in winter—can you tell me about a conversation or moment you shared with others during those times that stands out in your memory?

One night stands out, deep winter, when the wind was howling so hard it felt like the walls would give in. We’d finished work late, hands raw from breaking ice in the irrigation ditches. After dinner, a few of us crowded around the stove, legs tucked under us to catch the heat. Someone had managed to sneak a bit of dried tangerine peel from home, and we dropped it in the kettle to flavor the hot water. The steam smelled faintly of fruit, and for a moment it felt almost festive.

That night, someone started telling ghost stories—half to distract us from the cold, half to scare the new arrivals. But the talk shifted. One of the girls, usually quiet, started describing her old neighborhood in Shanghai—how the lights looked at dusk, the dumpling stall on the corner, the way her mother called her home from the alley. Suddenly everyone was sharing bits of their city lives, things we hadn’t dared mention out loud for weeks. For that hour, we made each other laugh and even cry a little, and the stove’s glow felt like a small piece of the world we’d lost. I remember thinking that as long as we could remember those details, we hadn’t completely disappeared into the mud and the cold. The next morning, no one talked about it. But that night, it was as if we’d built a secret room for ourselves, safe from everything outside.

The way you describe that night, with the tangerine peel and the stories, feels like a fragile space where you could all just be yourselves for a little while. After sharing those memories of home, did it change how you related to each other when you were back out in the fields or under the eyes of the team leaders?

It did, though not in any obvious way. We still had to keep our heads down and follow orders, and in front of the team leaders, we barely spoke except about work. But after that night, there was a quiet understanding between us. If someone stumbled or was struggling to keep up, you’d see another girl step in to help, or quietly pass along a bit of extra food if she had any. We started to notice each other’s moods more—if someone looked lost or on the verge of tears, you’d try to catch her eye and give a small smile when no one was watching. We didn’t talk about Shanghai openly, but sometimes a word or a look would be enough to remind us of that world, and it made us feel less alone. I think we became braver about holding on to our memories, even if we didn’t speak them out loud. It was like having a secret code, something that belonged only to us.

You notice how quickly people learn to read each other in a place like that. After that night, I started to sense when someone was about to break, even if she said nothing. There was a girl who hummed a city tune under her breath when she thought no one could hear; another would braid her hair the way she used to back home, even though it got her scolded. These were small rebellions, but they mattered. Sometimes, during the worst days in the fields—knees deep in mud, hands numb—I’d catch someone’s eye and we’d both remember that secret warmth around the stove. It didn’t change the work, or the way the leaders watched us, but it changed the way I carried myself. I knew I wasn’t the only one pretending not to miss my old life. That gave me a kind of stubbornness—not the kind you shout about, but the kind that keeps you from giving up when everything tells you to.

The image of those small rebellions—humming a tune, braiding hair—feels so powerful, like tiny ways of holding onto your identity when everything else is stripped away. Was there ever a moment when those quiet acts of defiance were noticed by someone in authority, and if so, how did you and the others respond?

There was one afternoon when the team leader caught a girl humming as we weeded the fields. He snapped at her, demanding to know what she was singing, and made her repeat the song out loud. The rest of us froze, heads down, pretending not to listen. She mumbled a few lines, her voice barely above a whisper, and he mocked her accent, calling it “bourgeois.” He made her stand at the edge of the field for the rest of the shift, not allowed to work or speak. That evening, the mood in our dorm was heavy—no one dared mention what had happened. But later, when the lights were out, someone quietly started humming the same tune, so softly it was almost just a breath. One by one, others joined in, just a note here and there, scattered through the darkness. It was a way of telling her, and each other, that we hadn’t given up that part of ourselves, no matter who was watching.

That kind of punishment was meant to break us, but it never quite worked the way they wanted. After that day, I noticed we became more careful, but also more determined. We stopped humming out loud in the fields, but in the evenings, when the wind drowned out our voices, we’d whisper the old city songs or recite lines from stories we remembered. If someone braided her hair, another would help her undo it quickly if footsteps approached. We learned to hide things in plain sight—folding a scrap of colored fabric into our pockets, drawing characters in the dirt with a stick, then smoothing them away before anyone saw. When authority noticed us, we shrank back, but in private we held tighter to the things that made us who we were. I realized then that even if they controlled our bodies, they couldn’t reach every corner of our minds. That stubbornness, that refusal to let go of small joys, became a quiet form of resistance. It made me wonder, sometimes, how much those in charge truly understood about the limits of their own power.

The idea that you found ways to resist in secret, even as you had to hide those parts of yourselves, really stays with me. You mentioned drawing characters in the dirt and reciting stories—was there a particular story, poem, or phrase that you found yourself returning to in those moments, something that helped you hold on when things felt unbearable?

There was a poem I learned as a child, lines about a traveler far from home, watching the moon and thinking of family. I used to whisper it to myself at night, especially when I felt most lost. The words were simple, but they carried the feeling of longing and endurance—“Raising my head, I gaze at the bright moon. Lowering it, I think of my hometown.” Sometimes, I’d write those characters in the dust on my bed platform with my finger, then brush them away before anyone noticed. The others had their own verses or sayings, but that one became my anchor. Just repeating it, silently or under my breath, reminded me that I wasn’t the first to feel this kind of distance, and that longing for home wasn’t something to be ashamed of. It made me feel connected—not just to my past, but to everyone who’d ever missed someone or someplace. That, more than anything, helped me endure.

I can still feel the shape of those words in my mouth, even now. Sometimes, if the moon was clear over the fields, I’d look up and let the poem run through my mind, almost like a prayer. It was a small act, but it kept me from disappearing into the sameness of every day. The others had their own lines—some from old stories, some just things their mothers used to say. We never spoke them out loud together, but you could tell when someone was repeating something for courage: the way her lips moved, or how she’d stare at the sky a little longer before going back to work. It’s strange how a few quiet words could make the difference between feeling like a shadow and remembering you were still a person, still yourself, no matter how far you’d been sent.

The image of you all silently holding onto different words—sometimes just moving your lips or pausing to look at the sky—makes me realize how much strength can come from things that are invisible to everyone else. Looking back now, do you think those private rituals and memories changed the kind of person you became after you left Beidahuang?
